passages.happening:
Pharisees and Sadducees come together to test Jesus. They ask him to show them a sign from heaven.

Jesus answers with the weather. In the evening they say, ‘The weather will be fair, for the sky is red,’ and in the morning, ‘Today it will be stormy, for the sky is red and overcast.’ “You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but not the signs of the times” (verse 3). Then he says, “A wicked and adulterous generation demands a sign, but none will be given it except the sign of Jonah” (verse 4). And he leaves them.
passages.hearers:
The Pharisees and the Sadducees did not usually stand together. The Pharisees were a movement of teachers devoted to keeping the law with care, and they kept many traditions handed down from earlier generations. The Sadducees were the party of the leading priestly families. They rejected those traditions, and they said “there is no resurrection” (22:23; Acts 23:8). Here the two rivals come side by side to test Jesus. Matthew is the Gospel that pairs them most often (3:7; 16:1-12).

A ‘sign from heaven’ meant a public wonder that would prove a leader came from God, on the asker's terms. Jesus had already refused the same demand (12:38-39). He has healed the sick and fed thousands. They want proof they can check and control.

A word on the weather lines in verses 2 and 3. Some of the oldest copies of Matthew, among them the two great fourth-century Bibles called Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, do not have them. Some scholars think the lines were added later from a similar saying in Luke (Luke 12:54-56). Others think copyists in places like Egypt, where a red morning sky does not bring rain, left them out because the saying did not fit their weather. Most modern Bibles print them with a note. Nothing in the meaning of the passage turns on it.
passages.ot:
The ‘sign of Jonah’ was explained in chapter 12. Jonah preached to Nineveh, and “the Ninevites believed God” (Jonah 3:5). And Jesus said, “as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” (12:40). The one sign they will get is his death and rising.

‘Adulterous’ is the prophets' word. They called Israel's turning from God to other loves unfaithfulness in marriage (Hosea 2; Jeremiah 3). The word speaks of a generation's heart toward God. It is not a judgment on the Jewish people as a whole.
passages.asks: The people who asked for a sign could read the sky but not what God was doing in front of them. Ask what proof you are still asking God for, and whether he has already given you more than enough to trust him.

passages.t: The leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees
passages.happening:
The disciples cross the lake and realise they have forgotten to bring bread. Jesus says, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees” (verse 6). They think he means the bread they forgot.

Jesus says, “You of little faith, why are you debating among yourselves about having no bread?” (verse 8). Do they not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets were left over? He was not talking about bread. Then they understand that he meant “the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Leaven, or yeast, was a lump of old dough kept back to make the next batch rise. A little works through the whole loaf. So it became a picture of influence. Jesus used it for the kingdom's hidden growth in 13:33. More often it stood for something that spreads and spoils.

Each Gospel names the leaven a little differently. Mark has “the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod” (Mark 8:15). Luke says the leaven of the Pharisees “is hypocrisy” (Luke 12:1). Only Matthew explains it as their teaching. The note on Mark 8 tells more.

Matthew also changes how the disciples come out of the scene. In Mark, the story ends with Jesus' question, “Do you still not understand?” (Mark 8:21). In Matthew, they do understand in the end (verse 12). And Jesus calls them ‘of little faith’, as he did in the storm (8:26) and to Peter on the water (14:31). ‘Little faith’ is not no faith. It is faith that forgets, for a moment, what it has seen.
passages.ot:
At Passover every Jewish home cleared out its leaven: “On the first day you are to remove the leaven from your houses” (Exodus 12:15). So leaven came to stand for what must be cleared away. Paul uses the same picture: “a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough” (1 Corinthians 5:6).

The forgotten bread also recalls the manna. God fed Israel in the desert day by day (Exodus 16:35). Jesus has now fed two crowds in the wilderness. The disciples are worried about one missing loaf.
passages.hard: Later Jesus will say of the scribes and Pharisees, “practice and observe everything they tell you” (23:3). How can he warn against their teaching here? Readers answer in more than one way. Many think the warning here is about something narrower than everything they taught: the unbelief that demanded a sign and could not see who was in front of them, and a way of reading Scripture that missed him. In chapter 23, Jesus speaks of what they read from Moses' law, while warning against how they lived. Others think Matthew's point in 23:3 is sharp irony. Either way, ‘teaching’ here is joined with the Sadducees, who differed from the Pharisees on much. What they shared, in this chapter, was the demand for a sign.
passages.asks: The disciples were anxious about bread while the one who fed thousands sat in the boat with them. Ask what you are worrying about this week as if Jesus were not there. And ask whose teaching is quietly working through your thinking like leaven, shaping you more than you know.

passages.t: You are the Christ, the Son of the living God
passages.happening:
Jesus comes to the region of Caesarea Philippi and asks his disciples, “Who do people say the Son of Man is?” (verse 13). They give the answers going round: John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.

“But what about you?” Jesus asks. “Who do you say I am?” (verse 15). Simon Peter answers, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (verse 16).

Jesus replies, “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah!” This was not revealed to Peter “by flesh and blood, but by My Father in heaven” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Caesarea Philippi lay well north of the Sea of Galilee, at the foot of Mount Hermon, by a spring that feeds the Jordan. A cave there held a shrine to the Greek god Pan. Herod the Great built a temple there in honour of the emperor Augustus, and his son Philip rebuilt the town and named it for Caesar. The note on Mark 8 tells more. It was a place full of other gods and of Rome's power. Here Peter names the Son of the living God.

‘Christ’ is the Greek form of the Hebrew word Messiah, ‘anointed one’, the king God had promised from David's family. Many Jews in Jesus' day hoped for such a king to drive out the foreign rulers. One Jewish writing from the century before Jesus, the Psalms of Solomon, prays for a son of David who would clear Jerusalem of the nations.

Matthew's account is fuller than Mark's. Only Matthew adds Jeremiah to the people's guesses. In Mark, Peter says, “You are the Christ” (Mark 8:29). In Matthew he adds, “the Son of the living God.” And only Matthew tells what Jesus says to Peter next, in verses 17 to 19.

‘Simon son of Jonah’ is Peter's own name and his father's. John's Gospel calls his father John (John 1:42), and the two may be forms of one name. ‘Flesh and blood’ was a Jewish way of saying ‘a human being’. Peter did not work this out, and no one told him. God showed him.
passages.ot: God promised David a son whose kingdom would last forever (2 Samuel 7:12-16), and a royal psalm says of the king, “You are My Son” (Psalm 2:7). ‘The living God’ is an Old Testament title for the God of Israel, set against idols that cannot see or hear. Hosea promised that those once called ‘not My people’ would be called “sons of the living God” (Hosea 1:10). At a place given over to Pan and to Caesar, Peter confesses Jesus as the Son of the God who is alive.
passages.asks: Jesus moves from ‘Who do people say?’ to ‘Who do you say?’ Opinions about Jesus are easy to report. He wants your own answer. And Peter's answer, Jesus says, was a gift from God, not a prize for being clever. If you are still unsure who Jesus is, you can ask God to show you. That is how Peter came to know.

passages.happening:
Jesus goes on: “And I tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it” (verse 18). He promises Peter the keys of the kingdom of heaven: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” (verse 19).

Then he tells the disciples not to tell anyone that he is the Christ.
passages.hearers:
Peter's name is a play on words. In Greek, Peter is Petros, and ‘rock’ is petra. In Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke, the word is kepha, which comes into our Bibles as Cephas (John 1:42). Simon's new name means Rock.

‘Church’ translates the Greek word ekklēsia, an assembly, the people called together. Matthew is the only Gospel to use the word (here and 18:17). Jesus calls it “My church.” It is his, and he builds it.

‘The gates of Hades’ was an old picture for the power of death. Hades was the Greek name for the realm of the dead, the word the Greek Old Testament used for the Hebrew Sheol. You can see this in the Bible itself: a psalm says “You will not abandon my soul to Sheol” (Psalm 16:10), and when Peter quotes it in Acts, it reads “Hades” (Acts 2:27). Hades is not the same as Gehenna, the word Jesus uses for hell. Jesus is saying that death itself will not overpower what he builds.

Keys belonged to a steward, a trusted servant who ran a household for its master and decided who could come in. To ‘bind’ and to ‘loose’ were words Jewish teachers used for forbidding and permitting, deciding what the law allowed. Rabbinic writings from after Jesus' time use the pair in just this way. Josephus, writing in the first century, says that when the Pharisees held power under Queen Alexandra, before Jesus' time, they bound and loosed as they pleased (Jewish War 1.111).

Two chapters later Jesus says the same words to the disciples together: “whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” (18:18). There it is about a church dealing with a member who has sinned.
passages.ot:
The key comes from Isaiah. God took the key of the royal household from one steward, Shebna, and gave it to another, Eliakim: “I will place on his shoulder the key to the house of David. What he opens no one can shut, and what he shuts no one can open” (Isaiah 22:22).

‘The gates of Sheol’ is the picture King Hezekiah used when he thought he was dying: “I must go through the gates of Sheol” (Isaiah 38:10).

The Old Testament also calls God himself a rock: “The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer” (Psalm 18:2). And God told Israel to “Look to the rock from which you were cut,” meaning Abraham (Isaiah 51:1-2). God had built a people on one man's faith before.
passages.hard:
Who or what is the rock? This is one of the great questions that divide Christian churches, and each answer is held by faithful people who know the text well. Here each is stated as its own teachers state it.

Catholic teaching reads the rock as Peter himself. The Catechism of the Catholic Church says that the Lord made Simon alone, whom he named Peter, the ‘rock’ of his church, and gave him the keys: authority to govern God's house, the church. The First Vatican Council (1870) taught that Christ gave Peter a true primacy of jurisdiction over the whole church, not only a place of honour, and that it continues in the bishops of Rome. Catholics point to the wordplay: you are Rock, and on this rock.

Orthodox teaching commonly reads the rock as the faith Peter confessed: that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God. John Chrysostom, the great preacher of the early church, explained ‘this rock’ as the faith of Peter's confession. The Orthodox honour Peter, but they do not accept the claim that the bishop of Rome governs the whole church.

Protestant teaching has often read the rock as Christ himself, or as the confession of him, pointing to Paul: “no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11). Many Protestant scholars today accept that the wordplay points to Peter in person, the first to confess and the leader of the first mission (Acts 2; 10). But they hold that a foundation is laid once (Ephesians 2:20), and that the text says nothing of successors.

All three agree on much. The church belongs to Christ, who builds it. Peter had a real leading place among the apostles. And the authority to bind and loose is given in 18:18 to the disciples together, though the churches differ on what that means for Peter's place. These notes do not decide between the readings. A reader from any of these churches should be able to recognise his own view here, and the others' as they are really held.
passages.asks: Jesus built his church on a man who, a few verses later, would get it badly wrong, and who would later deny him three times. Ask what that says about the kind of people Christ builds with. And notice the promise underneath every view: “I will build My church.” It does not finally rest on any of us.

passages.happening:
“From that time on” (verse 21), Jesus begins to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things at the hands of the elders, chief priests and scribes, be killed, and on the third day be raised to life.

Peter takes him aside and begins to rebuke him. “Far be it from You, Lord!” he says. “This shall never happen to You!” (verse 22).

Jesus turns and says to Peter, “Get behind Me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to Me. For you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
‘From that time on’ marks a turning point. Matthew used the same words when Jesus began to preach (4:17). The book now turns toward Jerusalem and the cross.

The elders, chief priests and scribes together made up the ruling council in Jerusalem. Jesus is saying that Israel's own leaders will reject him. A Messiah was supposed to win. Paul could still say years later that a crucified Messiah was “a stumbling block to Jews” (1 Corinthians 1:23). Peter is not being wicked. He loves Jesus and thinks he is protecting him.

Matthew adds a word to Mark's account. Jesus calls Peter a ‘stumbling block’, in Greek skandalon, a stone that trips people up. A few verses earlier Peter was the rock. Now the same man is a rock in the road.

‘Get behind Me’ shares its Greek words for ‘behind Me’ with Jesus' first call, ‘Come, follow Me’, which is literally ‘come behind Me’ (4:19). Jesus is sending Peter back to his place as a follower, behind him and not in front. ‘Satan’ means ‘adversary’. In the desert Satan offered Jesus the kingdoms of the world without the cross, and Jesus said, “Away from Me, Satan!” (4:10). Peter, without meaning to, is offering the same thing.
passages.ot: The word ‘must’ points to God's plan in Scripture. Isaiah spoke of a servant who “was pierced for our transgressions” and “crushed for our iniquities” (Isaiah 53:5). A psalm says, “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Psalm 118:22). And Daniel saw “One like the Son of Man” given a kingdom that would never be destroyed (Daniel 7:13-14). Jesus joins the glory of Daniel's Son of Man to the suffering of Isaiah's servant.
passages.hard:
Is Jesus calling Peter evil, or a tool of the devil? Not in the way it first sounds. Jesus does not say Peter is wicked, and he does not cast him off. He names where the thought comes from. Peter's words, kind as they are meant, repeat the oldest temptation Jesus faced: take the crown and skip the cross. Peter is still the rock of verse 18, still among the Twelve, and six days later he is on the mountain with Jesus (17:1). A good man can say a wrong thing with love in his heart. Jesus' rebuke is sharp because the stakes are high, not because Peter is lost.

Did Jesus really foresee his death and rising, or did the church add these words later? Some scholars since about 1900 have argued that the sayings were shaped after Easter. Others argue that Jesus, who knew the fate of the prophets and of John the Baptist, could well foresee his death. Christians have always held that Jesus knew where he was going and went there on purpose. Matthew says he ‘must’.
passages.asks: Peter wanted a Jesus who would not suffer, and a road for himself without pain. Most of us want the same. Ask where you have tried to keep Jesus' blessings while refusing his way. And if you have been rebuked, by God or by a friend, remember that Peter was not sent away. He was sent back behind Jesus, to follow.

passages.happening:
Jesus tells his disciples, “If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me” (verse 24). Whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for Jesus' sake will find it. What will it profit a man to gain the whole world and lose his soul? What can he give in exchange for it?

The Son of Man will come in his Father's glory with his angels, and “then He will repay each one according to what he has done” (verse 27). And Jesus adds, “Truly I tell you, some who are standing here will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in His kingdom” (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
To Jesus' hearers the cross meant one thing: the Roman death for slaves and rebels. After Herod the Great died in 4 BC, the Roman governor Varus put down a revolt and, Josephus says, crucified about two thousand men. A condemned man carried his own cross to the place of death. The Greek writer Plutarch mentions it in passing: every criminal who is punished carries his own cross. In 1968 a bone box was found in a tomb in Jerusalem holding the heel bone of a crucified man named Yehohanan, with an iron nail still in it. The note on Mark 8 tells more. ‘Take up your cross’ meant: walk the road of a condemned man.

The word Jesus uses for ‘life’ and for ‘soul’ is the same Greek word, psychē. Clutch your life, and you lose your soul. Give your life away, and you find it.

Matthew tells this as Mark does, with small changes. Mark says ‘for My sake and for the gospel’ (Mark 8:35); Matthew says ‘for My sake’. Mark speaks of being ashamed of Jesus; Matthew speaks of Jesus repaying each person for what he has done. And the last verse is sharper. Mark says some will see “the kingdom of God arrive with power” (Mark 9:1). Matthew says they will see “the Son of Man coming in His kingdom.”

‘Taste death’ simply means ‘die’.
passages.ot:
A psalm says that no one can pay God the price of a life: “For the redemption of his soul is costly, and never can payment suffice” (Psalm 49:8). Jesus asks the same question in the language of trade.

The judge who repays is the God of the psalms: “You will repay each man according to his deeds” (Psalm 62:12). Jesus says the Son of Man will do it. And ‘the Son of Man coming in His kingdom’ points back to Daniel, who saw “One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven” and given a kingdom (Daniel 7:13-14).
passages.hard:
Two hard things sit in these verses.

First, ‘deny himself’ and ‘take up his cross’. They do not mean hating yourself. They mean saying no to self as master: the self is not destroyed, it is handed over. Paul put it this way: “I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). And taking up your cross is not a command to stay where someone is harming you. The cross Jesus speaks of is the cost of following him. It is not abuse at another person's hands, and no one should be told to bear abuse as their cross. If you are being abused, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counsellor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line.

Second, verse 28. Some would not die before seeing ‘the Son of Man coming in His kingdom’. If Jesus meant his return at the end of the world, it did not happen in their lifetime. The philosopher Bertrand Russell, in his lecture Why I Am Not a Christian (1927), made this objection: that Jesus expected to return while people then living were still alive. Christians have read the verse in several ways, as the note on Mark 9:1 explains. Some point to what follows at once: six days later three of the disciples see Jesus' glory on the mountain (17:1-2). Some point to his rising from the dead, when he says “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me” (28:18), and to the coming of the Spirit. Some read it of the judgment that fell on Jerusalem when the Romans destroyed it in AD 70, within a generation, a coming in judgment rather than the final return. Christians have held each of these views. Matthew placed the saying right before the mountain, which suggests he saw at least a first answer there. These notes do not decide between them.
passages.asks: Jesus says this to all his disciples, not to a few heroes. Following him costs everyone something. Ask what ‘saving your life’ looks like for you: comfort, reputation, control. And ask what it would mean this week to lose it for his sake, and find it.
